# Mitsubishi L200 Warrior Rear Electric Window Issue

When the rear window stops responding on a Mitsubishi L200 Warrior, the problem rarely lies solely in the glass motor itself. The vehicle's architecture treats the interior courtesy lights and power windows as part of a shared electrical domain, often governed by specific fuse clusters or Body Control Module (BCM) logic. If your interior light between the front and rear seats has also failed while the mirror-mounted reader lamp remains functional, you are looking at a localized circuit failure rather than a total system-wide blackout.

The fact that the mirror light works confirms that the main battery feed is intact. This isolates the fault to the specific branch circuit controlling the rear cabin illumination and window switches. In many L200 models of this era, the fuse for the rear window and the interior dome lights are frequently housed in the same panel, often located under the dashboard near the driver's side kick panel or within the engine bay box depending on the specific year variant. Since you have already identified the interior light fuse but cannot locate the dedicated rear window fuse, it is highly probable that these two loads share a single fused relay circuit.

To troubleshoot this effectively, treat the system as a logical graph where nodes represent components and edges represent wiring paths. The loss of both the rear dome light and the rear window motor suggests they may be tied to the same 15A or 20A fuse. Check the documentation for your specific Warrior year; some models route these through a "Interior/Power" combined fuse, while others might use separate slots that happen to fail simultaneously if a solder bridge breaks in the loom.

Regarding the parking sensors, the situation is distinct because they were aftermarket additions. These modules usually do not integrate with the factory BCM unless hardwired into a CAN bus or a specific chassis ground point. If the sensors have failed now, it is likely due to a poor ground connection, a voltage drop caused by the same fuse issue affecting low-power circuits, or a loose connector at the bumper module. Since these were not factory fitted, there is no standard wiring diagram to reference. The most common pitfall here is assuming the sensors share power with the window system; they typically pull from an accessory (ACC) fused line that switches only when the ignition is on.

If you cannot physically locate a separate fuse for the rear window, verify whether the window operates via a direct ground path through the door switch or if it relies on a switched 12V feed from the fuse box. A multimeter check at the window motor connector with the key in the ON position will reveal if voltage is present. If you see 12V at the input terminal but no movement, the issue is mechanical binding or a failed motor coil. If there is no voltage, trace back to the switch assembly and the fuse panel.

The correlation between the dead dome light and the dead window strongly points to a common power source failure. Before replacing expensive components like the window motors or switches, ensure the shared fuse is intact and that the ground strap at the body chassis isn't corroded. Aftermarket sensor installations often introduce noise into the electrical system; if the sensors are shorting out a ground line, it could theoretically affect other circuits sharing that earth point, though this is less common than a simple blown fuse or loose connector.

Always prioritize checking fuses and grounds before replacing motors to avoid unnecessary part costs.
